content.text: Rates of reaction
Recall: what do bubbles show, and how do particles move in a solution?

elements.name: Photo
elements.alt: A flask of dilute hydrochloric acid with magnesium ribbon reacting inside, with rising gas bubbles clearly visible.
elements.request: Magnesium ribbon reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid in a flask. magnesium ribbon. colourless solution. gas bubbles

content.text: Today we are learning to
Calculate the mean rate of reaction from the volume of gas produced over a measured time, using cm³/s.
Describe how to investigate the effect of hydrochloric acid concentration on its reaction with magnesium, measuring gas volume over time and controlling the mass of magnesium and temperature.
Explain why increasing hydrochloric acid concentration increases the rate of reaction with magnesium, using collision theory and the frequency of successful collisions.
Make a prediction

Two flasks contain equal masses of magnesium and equal volumes of hydrochloric acid at the same temperature. One acid is twice as concentrated. Predict which produces 20 cm³ of gas first. Explain to a partner.

slides.notes:
Running
Give pupils 1 minute to think alone, then 2 minutes to explain their prediction to a partner. Take a few responses and ask pupils to justify them using particle collisions.

Answers
The flask with the more concentrated hydrochloric acid should produce 20 cm³ of gas first. Its greater concentration means more acid particles collide with the magnesium each second, so there are more successful collisions.

Misconceptions
Some pupils may predict that the more concentrated acid produces more total gas, rather than producing gas faster. Explain that concentration affects the rate; with equal magnesium masses and enough acid, the same amount of magnesium can produce the same final volume of hydrogen.

Background
This prediction links the practical comparison to collision theory: the independent variable is acid concentration, while magnesium mass, acid volume and temperature are kept the same.

content.text: Measure hydrogen over time
Magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
Add magnesium, fit the bung and start timing promptly.
Record gas volume every 10 seconds until it stops rising.
Repeat with different acid concentrations.

elements.name: Photo
elements.alt: A conical flask containing hydrochloric acid and magnesium is sealed with a bung and connected by a delivery tube to a horizontal gas syringe held by a clamp stand.
elements.request: A conical flask containing hydrochloric acid and magnesium, sealed with a bung; a delivery tube connects it to a horizontal clamped gas syringe whose plunger can move freely.. Gas syringe. Clamp stand. Delivery tube. Bung

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 5 minutes establishing the method. Ask pupils to identify how gas reaches the syringe and to rehearse the sequence in pairs. If carrying out the practical, demonstrate the setup and prompt pupils to record volumes every 10 seconds.

Misconceptions
A bung fitted before timing starts can allow some gas to escape before measurement begins, making the recorded volume too low. Emphasise fitting the bung and starting the timer promptly. A leak also makes the measured gas volume unreliable.

Background
The reaction is Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. The gas syringe measures hydrogen volume directly. Taking readings at regular intervals allows pupils to compare how quickly gas is produced.

content.text: Make the comparison fair and safe
Change only the hydrochloric acid concentration.
Control:
Keep magnesium mass and surface area, acid volume and temperature the same.
Improve:
Use excess acid, check for leaks and repeat each concentration three times.
Protect:
Wear eye protection. Keep hydrogen away from flames.

slides.notes:
Running
Allow about 4 minutes. In pairs, pupils identify the variable changed, the controls and the safety precautions. Take answers and check why each control matters.

Misconceptions
Changing magnesium mass as well as acid concentration would make it impossible to attribute a rate difference to concentration alone. A larger magnesium surface area can also increase rate. Explain that only the independent variable should change; control magnesium mass and surface area, acid volume and temperature. Hydrogen is flammable, so keep it away from flames.

Background
Repeating each concentration helps identify anomalous results and makes a mean rate more reliable. Using excess acid helps ensure magnesium is the limiting reactant, so differences in final gas volume are not caused by running out of acid.

content.text: Worked example: mean rate
Find the mean rate over the first 40 seconds.
Mean rate = gas volume ÷ time
Volume produced = 60 − 0 = 60 cm³
Mean rate = 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5 cm³/s

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: At zero seconds the volume is zero cubic centimetres; at 40 seconds it is 60 cubic centimetres.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 3 minutes modelling the subtraction of initial from final volume and time. Ask pupils to say the units aloud and check the calculation with the class.

Misconceptions
Some pupils may divide by the final time without first finding the change in gas volume, or may give a rate in cm³ rather than cm³/s. Reinforce that mean rate is change in volume divided by change in time: (60 − 0) ÷ (40 − 0) = 1.5 cm³/s.

Background
This is the average rate across the chosen time interval, not the rate at every moment. The reaction is usually fastest near the start and slows as reactants are used up.

content.text: Calculate the mean rate
A reaction produces 0 cm³ at 0 s and 80 cm³ at 40 s. Calculate its mean rate over these 40 seconds.
A second reaction produces 0 cm³ at 0 s and 60 cm³ at 50 s. Calculate its mean rate over these 50 seconds.
Which reaction has the greater mean rate over its measured interval? Use your answers.
Write the calculation and give each rate in cm³/s.

slides.notes:
Running
Give pupils about 5 minutes to calculate independently, showing working and units. Then have pairs compare answers and explain which rate is greater before checking as a class.

Answers
1. 80 ÷ 40 = 2 cm³/s.
2. 60 ÷ 50 = 1.2 cm³/s.
3. The first reaction has the greater mean rate: 2 cm³/s is greater than 1.2 cm³/s.

Misconceptions
A larger final volume does not necessarily mean a faster reaction. Compare volume produced per second: the second reaction produces 60 cm³, but takes 50 seconds. Keep the units as cm³/s.

Background
Mean rate comparisons are only meaningful when the measured intervals are clear. Here each rate is calculated over its stated interval; the comparison is between those average rates.

content.text: Why does concentration affect rate?
Higher concentration means more acid particles in the same volume.
Particles collide with the magnesium surface more often.
Successful collisions have enough energy to react.
More successful collisions each second give a faster reaction.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: Two equal-volume solution panels at the same temperature show twice as many acid particles in the higher-concentration panel beside identical magnesium surfaces, with matching motion arrows.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 4 minutes talking through the particle explanation. Ask pupils to describe what changes between the two concentrations and connect that change to successful collisions each second.

Misconceptions
Pupils may think successful collisions are guaranteed whenever particles collide. Clarify that a collision must have enough energy to react; increasing concentration raises the frequency of collisions and therefore the number of successful collisions each second.

Background
Collision theory explains reaction rate in terms of the frequency of successful collisions. For magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid, acid particles collide with the magnesium surface.

content.text: More particles, not faster particles
Both solutions are at 20 °C. Doubling concentration does not double particle speed.
Unchanged: The particles have the same average kinetic energy.
Changed: More acid particles reach the magnesium each second.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: Equal-sized panels compare dilute and concentrated hydrochloric acid at 20 °C, with twice as many particles but matching motion-arrow lengths and equal magnesium surfaces.

slides.notes:
Running
Allow about 3 minutes. Ask pupils to explain which property stays the same and which changes, then correct any claim that concentration makes particles faster.

Misconceptions
Some pupils may think concentrated acid reacts faster because its particles move faster or have more kinetic energy. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is unchanged; the higher concentration means more particles reach the magnesium surface each second.

Background
Temperature and concentration affect rate in different ways. Raising temperature increases average particle kinetic energy; raising concentration at the same temperature increases the number of particles per unit volume.

content.text: Choose the best explanation
Why does more concentrated acid react faster with identical magnesium at the same temperature?
A
Every collision now causes a reaction.
B
There are more successful collisions each second.
C
Each acid particle has more energy.
D
The acid particles move faster.

slides.notes:
Running
Give pupils about 3 minutes to choose an answer independently and justify it. Ask them to explain why one distractor is wrong before confirming B.

Answers
B: There are more successful collisions each second.

Misconceptions
A says every collision reacts; many collisions lack enough energy. C says each particle has more energy; concentration does not increase average kinetic energy. D says particles move faster; at the same temperature their average speed is not increased by concentration. The correct explanation is B: more frequent collisions produce more successful collisions each second.

Background
This question checks the distinction between collision frequency and collision energy. The latter is affected by temperature, while concentration changes how many particles are available to collide.

content.text: Evaluate a new investigation
In 30 s, 0.5 mol/dm³ acid gives 24 cm³ of gas and 1.0 mol/dm³ acid gives 42 cm³. Both start at 0 cm³. Calculate both mean rates.
The tests used 0.04 g and 0.08 g of magnesium respectively. Explain why the rates cannot show the effect of concentration alone. State two controls for a repeat.
Stretch: with equal magnesium masses, excess acid and equal temperatures, predict how concentration affects the time to finish and the final gas volume. Explain.
Calculate, evaluate and justify.

slides.notes:
Running
Allow about 8 minutes for pupils to calculate, evaluate the comparison and suggest controls. Invite pupils to attempt the stretch, then review answers and require them to justify the predicted final volume.

Answers
1. 24 ÷ 30 = 0.8 cm³/s for 0.5 mol/dm³ acid; 42 ÷ 30 = 1.4 cm³/s for 1.0 mol/dm³ acid.
2. The magnesium masses were different, so concentration was not the only variable. More magnesium can produce gas differently and changes the comparison; the results cannot show the effect of concentration alone.
3. Any two suitable controls: magnesium mass, magnesium surface area, acid volume or temperature. For a fair comparison, use the same value for each test.
4. With equal magnesium masses, excess acid and equal temperatures, the more concentrated acid should finish reacting sooner because its rate is higher. The final gas volume should be the same because the same amount of magnesium reacts and produces the same amount of hydrogen.

Misconceptions
Pupils may assume the larger gas volume at 30 seconds proves a larger final yield; it only shows more gas was collected by that time. The unequal magnesium masses also confound the comparison. Explain that a fair repeat must use equal magnesium masses and control other relevant variables.

Background
The gas volume at a fixed time can be used to compare mean rates, but it does not by itself establish the final yield. Magnesium and hydrochloric acid react in a 1:2 mole ratio, and the hydrogen yield depends on the limiting reactant.

content.text: Optional Higher: rate at one instant

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: Gas volume rises and levels off. A tangent at 20 seconds passes through zero seconds, 12 cubic centimetres, and 40 seconds, 60 cubic centimetres.

content.text: Use the tangent’s points (0 s, 12 cm³) and (40 s, 60 cm³) to calculate the rate at 20 s.

slides.notes:
Running
Allow about 4 minutes for pupils who are ready for the extension. Ask them to use the tangent’s two points, show the gradient calculation and include cm³/s.

Answers
(60 − 12) ÷ (40 − 0) = 48 ÷ 40 = 1.2 cm³/s.

Misconceptions
Pupils may use the overall curve’s start and end points instead of the stated tangent points. For an instantaneous rate, use the gradient of the tangent: change in volume divided by change in time.

Background
The gradient of a volume–time graph gives reaction rate. A tangent estimates the gradient at one instant, while a secant between two points on the curve gives a mean rate over an interval.
